title: What a Network Is Made Of
lead: The role of every box in the network — router, switch, firewall, IPS, access point, WLC, server, endpoint — and how PoE feeds half of them.

blocks.text: The exam almost never asks "what is a router." It asks it differently: *which device do you need to place to get this specific effect*. So for every box, keep exactly three things in mind:

items: **At what layer it makes its forwarding decision** — by MAC address (L2), by IP address (L3), or by session content (L4–L7).
**What it does with broadcast traffic** — forwards it or stops it.
**What it gives you that the device one layer down doesn't.**

blocks.text: These three answers are enough to tell the correct option from the plausible-sounding one.
A switch operates at **Layer 2**: it looks at the destination MAC address in the frame header and sends the frame out the port where that MAC was last seen.

items: Every switch port is its **own collision domain**. That's exactly what distinguishes it from the old hub, where all ports shared one collision domain and interfered with each other.
All ports in the same VLAN are **one broadcast domain**. A switch doesn't stop broadcast traffic — it replicates it out every port in the VLAN.
It builds its own MAC table by learning the **source MAC** of incoming frames, and ages entries out on a timer (300 seconds by default).
A frame with an unknown destination MAC gets **flooded** out every port in the VLAN except the one it arrived on. That's not a malfunction — it's normal behavior (unknown unicast flooding).

blocks.text: An **L3 switch** (multilayer switch, MLS) is a switch that can also route between VLANs through an SVI (`interface vlan 10`). You reach for one when you need inter-VLAN routing at line rate inside a building, rather than over a link to a router.

blocks.title: Trap
paras: "A switch divides the network into collision domains, a router into broadcast domains." This line shows up in dozens of disguises. An L3 switch divides both: each VLAN on it is its own broadcast domain.

blocks.text: A router makes its decision based on the **destination IP address** and the routing table, choosing the route with the longest matching prefix (longest prefix match).

items: Every router interface is its **own broadcast domain**. Broadcast traffic doesn't cross a router: it forwards neither L2 broadcasts nor (by default) IP broadcasts.
A router connects **different networks/subnets** and different Layer 2 technologies — Ethernet on one side, serial/fiber/cellular on the other.
It's also where NAT, ACLs, QoS policies, DHCP relay, and tunnels live.

blocks.text: A regular **stateful firewall** tracks connection *state*: it remembers that a TCP SYN went out from the inside, and lets back in only the reply belonging to that specific session. That's what sets it apart from an ACL on a router, which examines each packet individually, with no memory of the session.
**NGFW** (next-generation firewall) adds on top of that:

items: application identification independent of port (Facebook runs on 443 — a plain firewall sees "https," an NGFW sees "Facebook");
rules tied to users, not just IP addresses;
built-in IPS and TLS inspection;
reputation feeds and malware protection (AMP).

head: IDS
IPS
rows: "off to the side," receives a copy of the traffic (SPAN/TAP)

blocks.text: **NGIPS** — the same thing, but with context: it knows what OSes and applications are on the network and doesn't waste Windows signatures on a Linux server.

An access point is a **bridge between radio and wire**: it turns 802.11 frames into 802.3 frames and back. The radio channel is a shared medium using CSMA/CA, so all clients of one AP on one channel share its bandwidth.
Two ways APs can operate:

items: **Autonomous** — the AP is its own controller, with configuration stored on each AP individually. Fine for 3–5 APs; beyond that, administration becomes a nightmare.

**Lightweight** — the AP holds no configuration of its own; it brings up a **CAPWAP** tunnel to a WLC and gets everything from it: SSID, channels, power, policies. This is how networks of dozens of APs are built.

blocks.text: A WLC (wireless LAN controller) centralizes management: RRM (automatic channel and power selection), client roaming between APs, applying QoS and security policies, a single point of monitoring.

blocks.title: Remember
paras: An access point by itself is an **L2** device. It doesn't route and doesn't assign addresses; the client gets its IP from DHCP on the wired network.

items: **Endpoint** — anything that generates and consumes traffic at the edge of the network: a PC, phone, printer, IP camera, IoT sensor.
**Server** — an endpoint that other devices talk to: DHCP, DNS, file, web, domain controller.

**Hypervisor** — the layer that splits one physical server into several virtual machines: it hands each VM its share of CPU, memory, disk, and network, and isolates VMs from each other. Type 1 (bare-metal — ESXi, Hyper-V) installs directly on the hardware; type 2 (VirtualBox, VMware Workstation) runs on top of a regular OS.
Inside the hypervisor runs a **virtual switch** (vSwitch): the VMs' virtual NICs plug into it, and the server's physical NIC serves as the uplink to the real network.

blocks.text: Power over Ethernet feeds access points, IP phones, and cameras over the same cable that carries data — no separate outlet needed near the ceiling.
A switch first **detects** the powered device (by probing for a 25 kΩ resistance), then negotiates a power class — either via electrical class or via CDP/LLDP-MED.

Hence the standard exam question about **auto mode vs. static mode**: in auto, the port reserves exactly what the device requested during negotiation, and the remaining budget stays available to other ports. In static, the administrator hard-reserves a fixed amount of power regardless of actual consumption — predictable, but it wastes budget.

SW1# show power inline
Available:370.0(w)  Used:60.4(w)  Remaining:309.6(w)

Interface Admin  Oper       Power   Device              Class Max
                            (Watts)
--------- ------ ---------- ------- ------------------- ----- ----
Gi1/0/1   auto   on         30.0    AIR-AP2802I-E-K9    4     30.0
Gi1/0/2   auto   on         15.4    IP Phone 7841       3     30.0
Gi1/0/3   auto   off        0.0     n/a                 n/a   30.0

sections.title: Inside the switch: what stands behind "ports"

blocks.text: When a question lists model numbers, three genuinely different things sit behind them.

**Stack (StackWise).** Several physical switches are connected with stacking cables and act as **one device**: one management IP, one configuration, one STP instance, ports numbered `Gi1/0/1`, `Gi2/0/1` by stack-member number. Losing one member doesn't take down the stack. That's why the correct answer to "how do you simplify managing 5 switches in a rack" is to stack them, not configure each one separately.

**Modularity.** A chassis with line cards vs. a fixed-configuration switch: the former survives changing port types and scaling up, the latter is cheaper. Uplink ports are almost always faster than user-facing ports (48 × 1G down, 4 × 10G up) — that's not decoration, it's an oversubscription calculation: if all 48 gigabit ports were busy at once, four 10-gigabit uplinks would deliver 40 Gbps against 48 Gbps of load.

**Buffering and switching speed.** Questions mention "wire speed / line rate" — a switch that can handle traffic on every port simultaneously with no loss. If it can't (oversubscription), frames get buffered and dropped when the buffer fills.

sections.title: Inside the router: RIB and FIB

blocks.text: A router keeps two tables, and they get mixed up:

items: **RIB** (routing information base) — what `show ip route` displays: every known route with its source, administrative distance, and metric. This is the output of the **control plane**.

**FIB** (forwarding information base) — what packets actually get forwarded by: a precomputed distillation of the RIB plus an adjacency table (next-hop MAC addresses). This is the **data plane** — on Cisco it's CEF, and it runs in hardware.

blocks.text:
R1# show ip route 10.10.13.7          ! RIB — "which route was chosen and why"
R1# show ip cef 10.10.13.7            ! FIB — "where the packet goes right now"

Practical implication: a route can be present in the RIB and still not work if the adjacency to the next hop hasn't resolved (no ARP). The reverse also happens after a failure — a mismatch between RIB and FIB is fixed with `clear ip route *`.

The second thing a router gives you is **different interface types on one device**: Ethernet on the inside, fiber or serial on the outside, tunnels, VLAN subinterfaces, and a loopback as the device's own stable address. A loopback never "goes down" physically, which is why it's used as the router ID and as the management address.

sections.title: Where security tools sit in the topology

blocks.text:
Internet
      │
   [ Router ]  ── edge, NAT, basic ACLs
      │
   [ NGFW ]    ── application- and user-based policy
      │   └──── [ DMZ ]  public-facing servers
      │
   [ Core / Distribution ]  ── ACLs between segments
      │
   [ Access ]  ── port security, DHCP snooping, 802.1X
      │
   endpoints
The placement logic, tested with wording like "where should the device be placed":

items: **Firewall/NGFW** — at the boundary between zones of different trust: internet ↔ DMZ ↔ internal network. Inside a single segment it's useless — traffic never passes through it.
**IPS** — inline on the path of critical traffic; **IDS** — off to the side, on a SPAN port.
**DMZ** — a segment for whatever is reached from outside: mail relay, web server. Access from the DMZ into the internal network is blocked; the reverse is restricted.
**Proxy** — wherever you need control over users' web access and caching.
**Load balancer** — in front of a server farm; distributes sessions and checks node health.
**VPN concentrator** — at the edge, often the same box as the firewall.

sections.title: PoE in more detail: budget, classes, and diagnostics

blocks.text: Every PoE switch has a **shared power budget** (370 W and up on most models) — a separate resource split across ports. That's exactly why the auto/static question isn't about "how much the device consumes," but about **what happens to the leftover budget**.
Negotiation sequence:

items: **Detection** — the switch applies a small voltage and looks for the characteristic 25 kΩ resistance. If it's not there, no power is supplied at all (protection against frying a non-PoE device).
**Classification** — the requested power is determined from the electrical class (0–8).
**Further negotiation via CDP/LLDP-MED** — the device can specify its needs more precisely than the class allows, and the switch adjusts the reservation accordingly.

head: Class
Max per port
Typical device
rows: undetermined, defaults to the af maximum

blocks.text: Diagnosing "the device won't power on":

SW1# show power inline                       ! overall budget and what's allocated to whom
SW1# show power inline gigabitethernet1/0/1 detail
SW1# show interfaces gigabitethernet1/0/1 status
Port      Name     Status       Vlan  Duplex  Speed Type
Gi1/0/1   AP-2F-01 notconnect   60    auto    auto  10/100/1000BaseTX

Check, in order: whether a power class was negotiated and how much (`show power inline`), whether the **overall** budget has room (`Available`), whether power is disabled on the port (`power inline never`), whether the device is exceeding its class (the port goes `err-disabled` with the reason `inline-power`), and finally — whether the cable can carry it (for 802.3bt, cable category and the integrity of all four pairs matter).

interface GigabitEthernet1/0/1
 power inline auto max 30000        ! cap the port at 30 W
 power inline police                 ! shut the port down on overdraw

blocks.text: Hubs and repeaters rarely show up as correct answers on the modern exam — they exist to help you tell collision domains apart from broadcast domains.

sections.title: Counting domains on a diagram: a worked problem

blocks.text: The diagram from the question, and the two counts it asks for.

[ Router R1 ]
                  Gi0/0   Gi0/1
                    │       │
             ┌──────┘       └──────┐
        [ SW1 ]                [ SW2 ]
      4 ports: PC1..PC4      3 ports: PC5..PC7
      all in VLAN 1           VLAN 10: PC5, PC6
                             VLAN 20: PC7
                                 │
                              [ HUB ]
                            PC8, PC9, PC10
**Collision domains.** Count every point-to-point link and every switch port:

items: SW1: 4 ports to PCs + 1 uplink to R1 = **5**;
SW2: 3 ports to PCs/hub + 1 uplink = **4**, but the port the hub plugs into shares a domain with the PCs behind the hub;
the hub as a whole — **1** domain covering all of its ports.

blocks.text: Total: 5 + 3 (SW2's ports to PC5, PC6, and the uplink) + 1 (the port to the hub, together with PC8–PC10) = **9**. Rule: **a switch port is its own domain; a hub is one domain for everything attached to it**.
**Broadcast domains.** Count VLANs and router interfaces:

items: the network behind SW1 — one VLAN 1 → **1** domain;
behind SW2 — VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 → **2** domains; the hub inside VLAN 20 doesn't create a separate domain.

blocks.text: Total: **3**. Every router interface is a boundary; every VLAN is a separate domain within the switched network.

blocks.title: Trap
paras: A hub adds devices to an **existing** broadcast domain and does **not** increase how many there are. "A hub splits the network" is the most common wrong answer in these problems.

sections.title: Switch, router, L3 switch: summary table

blocks.text: Hence the simple rule for these questions: **the L3 switch routes inside the building, the router faces outward**.

sections.title: How to read a diagram in a question

blocks.text: Half of the questions with a diagram are solved by reading the picture, not by calculating.

items: **Identify the role of each icon** — a router is drawn as a circle with arrows, a switch as a rectangle with arrows, a cloud is someone else's network (the internet or a provider).
**Find the subnet boundaries** — every line between routers is a separate subnet; everything behind a switch is usually one subnet per VLAN.
**Look at the interface labels** — they tell you which side to count addresses from.
**Determine what's being asked**: a packet's path, a missing configuration, a device type.

blocks.text: Check yourself: if you can't say, from the diagram, how many **broadcast domains** it contains, you haven't finished reading the device roles yet.

items: "Which device permits or denies network traffic based on a set of rules?" — firewall, if it's about policy and session state; ACL, if it's about a list on a router interface.
"What is a network appliance that checks the state of a packet…" — **stateful firewall** (the keyword is *state*).
"What is a role of access points in an enterprise network?" — connect wireless clients to the wired network (an L2 bridge), not "assign IP addresses" and not "route."
"Which role does a hypervisor provide for each virtual machine?" — allocates and isolates compute resources; the option "provides an OS" is wrong — the administrator installs the OS.
"What is an advantage of auto mode versus static mode for PoE?" — unused power stays in the shared budget for other ports.
Questions about **IDS vs. IPS** come down to one word: "inline" and "drops" → IPS.

blocks.title: Trap
paras: Answer choices often include "hub" and "repeater." On the modern exam these are always the wrong answer, except for a direct question about collision domains: a hub is one collision domain for everyone, half duplex, no filtering at all.

items.q: How many broadcast domains does a 24-port switch with a single VLAN have, and how many collision domains?
items.a: One broadcast domain and 24 collision domains — one per port.

items.q: A device receives a copy of traffic via SPAN and logs alerts but doesn't block anything. What is it?
items.a: IDS. An IPS sits inline and can drop the packet.

items.q: An access point got its settings from a controller over a tunnel. What's the protocol and the AP's mode called?
A PoE port in auto mode gave the AP 15.4 W out of a 30 W budget. What happens to the remaining 14.6 W?
items.a: It stays in the switch's shared budget and can be allocated to other ports.

items.q: How does an NGFW differ from a stateful firewall, in one sentence?
items.a: It sees the application and the user, not just addresses, ports, and session state.

items.q: How does the RIB differ from the FIB?
items.a: The RIB is all known routes with AD and metrics (control plane); the FIB is the precomputed forwarding table that packets are actually forwarded by (data plane).

items.q: Five switches in a rack need to be managed as a single device. What do you do?
items.a: Stack them: one management address, one configuration, one STP instance.

items.q: An access point won't power on even though the port is up. Three checks?
items.a: Whether detection and classification succeeded (show power inline), whether the switch's overall budget has room, and whether the port is restricted by power inline never or a max value.

items.q: Where do you connect an IDS and where do you connect an IPS?
items.a: IDS — on a SPAN port off to the side of the traffic; IPS — inline, on the traffic's path.

items.q: What is a DMZ, and why is a server published there instead of into the internal network?
items.a: A segment for services that need to be reachable from outside; access from it into the internal network is blocked, so compromising the published service doesn't grant access to the internal network.
